Quick observation on why AI has exploded at work, but has been slow to disrupt consumer apps:

At work, AI follows patterns and gets rid of drudgery (good!)

At home, AI follows patterns but it generates slop (bad!)

This is why AI has taken off at work, but not so much for consumer apps and experiences (social, entertainment, dating, etc)

Much of work is drudgery - filling out forms, following processes, writing updates, reviewing boilerplate code, etc. - and AI does a great job compressing this down the boring steps so that humans can focus on the high-leverage steps. The boring/routine work is not hard, but they often take a lot of steps and you have to stitch together a lot of data. You follow patterns. AI is good at following patterns too.

Consumer attention, on the other hand, is hard to win over because people crave novelty, seek parasocial relationships, and are so cognizant of AI slop. A video of an attractive person talking loses its ability to generate parasocial relationships. In domains like social media, video, etc where authenticity is paramount, a distorted AI sign in the background can ruin the entire thing. Novelty is generated by surfing the cultural wave with something new and unique - AI slop often pattern matches to the past, after all, it’s the past that’s in the data set, and as a result, new/unique is hard

This is a form of “adversarial creativity” - and it exists in business as well. When you think about inherently adversarial activities in business - like sales and marketing, where novel messaging, competitive move+countermove dominate - AI has received the most scrutiny for generating slop. No one wants the same sounding AI generated cold emails. No one wants to use AI slop software. You have to go outside the model in order to really land a message.

Perhaps this is the ultimate human-in-the-loop problem, because to do something fresh and unique requires adversarial creativity. Or maybe with enough advancements around being able to observe and react in real-time, future AI models will be able to say something novel by taking into account the X timeline from the past 24 hours.

One of the biggest things I learned was to stop following other people, especially very smart people. Smart people can be incredibly convincing. I prefer to read their research now rather than absorb their conviction directly.

In 2021 I got lured into the whole Cathie Wood trade. I wanted to take a break from markets and focus on meditation, and at the time I basically thought Cathie Wood was the Jesus of investing. So I put a huge amount of money into those stocks, stopped trading for around six months, and barely looked at my computer. When I finally came back, my portfolio was down around 50%.

The SPAC period taught me something similar. I didn’t lose a huge amount of money there, but I made plenty of mistakes simply because I was following trends instead of following what I actually understood.

Those experiences changed the way I invest. I don’t chase market trends anymore. I don’t take large positions in things I don’t understand extremely well. I generally avoid early-stage biotech before Phase 3, or keep it very small. And if I don’t have something I understand deeply, I’m perfectly happy to let the money do nothing.

I’ve also become much better at expressing my views with options in ways that give me less downside when I’m wrong. The biggest change is probably that I now concentrate heavily only when I understand the company, the situation, and the risk extremely well.

Lukas, is the purpose of life to become rich, or to become wiser, happier?

Usually when I meet people who got rich very quickly from Bitcoin or some one trick wonder, I notice something missing. They have money, but often they’re still confused, jumping from one experience to another because they can afford it: yachts, parties, drugs, women, whatever comes next.

And if you don’t know who I’m talking about, just go to Ibiza in the summer. You’ll meet plenty of them. Rich people getting drunk, getting high, jumping from one yacht to another, one party to another, one model to another, constantly looking for the next experience.

When you make money slowly, through struggle, something very different happens. You make mistakes. You learn. You calibrate. You learn to deal with fear, greed, ego, uncertainty, failure. You get knocked down and learn how to get back up. And those lessons don’t only make you a better investor. They make you stronger and better equipped to deal with problems everywhere else in life.

The struggle also teaches appreciation. A person who climbed the mountain will appreciate the view very differently from someone who arrived at the top in a helicopter.

The money is not the most valuable thing you gain. It’s the person you had to become to earn it.

Thats why from poor to rich the people who are most fulfilled are the ones who add the most value to others in the real sense 

That is the human contract and why when money is gained outside of this the person who acquires it compensates for this lack of mutual respect in a material sense as they are imposters 

The takeaway is when dealing with people have the mindset of how can you add value via mutual reciprocal respect - it strips away the falsehood that modern society has created
